newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries up at midday, boosted by core CPI.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries up at midday, boosted by core CPI.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices remained higher at midday on Tuesday, benefitting from a benign U.S. December inflation report.

Near the beginning of the trading session, the government reported that its December Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.3 percent, as forecast, but that the core CPI, the index without its more erratic food and energy components, rose just a slight 0.1 percent, a smaller increase than the 0.2 percent gain economists and the financial markets had anticipated.
The market rallied on the core CPI reading.

"It's primarily a CPI related move and it's the core component that people are focusing on," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "We did see some upward price pressure in the energy area but that didn't seem to bother people. They focused on the 0.1 percent increase in core inflation and that spurred the rally."
The benchmark 30-year bond was up 28/32 to 96-13/32, yielding 6.78 percent at midday.
At mid-morning, the bond briefly extended its gain to a full point, following subdued readings on area manufacturing activity by the Atlanta and Richmond Federal Reserve Banks.
A strong dollar was also positive for the Treasury market, analysts said.
"The higher dollar is helping out," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"The strong dollar is probably encouraging foreign buying, if not reflecting buying that's already taken place," said Moran.
The dollar was broadly higher at midday, even before U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated during a press briefing his belief "without question" in a strong dollar.

To score its advance, the market set aside a somewhat more robust report on December retail sales than economists, on average, had forecast. (Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.5 percent retail sales gain overall and a 0.4 percent rise excluding autos.)
"Retail sales increased a solid 0.6 percent in December, ... (leaving) the quarterly pattern decidedly better than expected," said Sally Kleinman, economist at Chase Economics Research.
"The retail sales numbers confirm that the consumer came back solidly in the fourth quarter," agreed Bankers Trust managing director and chief global markets economist John Williams.
Williams said if that momentum carries forward into 1997, inflation pressures will continue to build and eventually will show up in the CPI.

"That's why we think that if the Federal Reserve sees some upward pressure on the CPI and also in the Employment Cost Index due on January 28, it will tighten (monetary policy) in the spring," he said.
But Williams said the 0.1 percent core CPI rise that the government reported for December means that "for now, the burden of proof is on those of us who have that view."
In early trade, the BTM/Schroders index of chain store sales reflected a 0.3 percent decline, on the soft side.
Along the yield curve, two-year notes were up 4/32 to 99-18/32, yielding 5.99 percent.
Three- and six-month bill rates were each down two basis points to 5.04 percent and 5.09 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were down five basis points to 5.30 percent.
Five-year notes were up 11/32 to 99-7/32, yielding 6.31 percent.
Ten-year notes were up 19/32 to 99-24/32, yielding 6.53 percent.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
